summary.text: Loved by Zeus, Antiope — daughter of Nycteus, or of the river Asopus — passed to Epopeus of Sicyon, was brought home captive by her uncle Lycus, and bore twins on the road. Years later she slipped Dirce's chains; her sons tied Dirce to a bull, took Thebes, drove out Laius, and walled the city — Zethus hauling stone, Amphion's lyre drawing the rocks after him.

chapters.title: Whose daughter, whose sons
chapters.text: Antiope's beauty was famed through Greece, and Zeus lay with her. Apollodorus and Hyginus make her the daughter of Nycteus, and among the gods' deceits in Arachne's web Ovid shows Jupiter, in a satyr's shape, getting twins on Nycteus' lovely daughter. Homer calls her instead the daughter of Asopus, a woman who boasted of sleeping in Zeus' arms, and so does Apollonius. Pausanias knew both reports, and quotes an old epic poet for whom she was Asopus' daughter and conceived by Zeus and by Epopeus alike; at Sicyon, where her statue stood, the people claimed her sons as Sicyonians.

chapters.title: Flight to Sicyon
chapters.text: Pregnant and threatened by her father, Antiope fled to Sicyon and married its king, Epopeus, Apollodorus says; Nycteus killed himself in despair, charging his brother Lycus to punish them both, and Lycus took Sicyon, slew Epopeus and led her home a captive. Hyginus agrees in outline, though his Sicyonian bears another name. Pausanias says Epopeus carried her off, and in the battle that followed both leaders were wounded; Nycteus, carried home to die, made Lycus regent for the boy Labdacus and begged him for vengeance. But Epopeus died of the wound he had neglected, and his successor Lamedon gave Antiope up without a war.

chapters.title: Born on the road
chapters.text: Led back toward Thebes, Antiope gave birth on the road at Eleutherae, under Cithaeron; the babies were exposed, and a cowherd found and reared them, naming them Zethus and Amphion. Pausanias saw the small cave where, by local story, she laid them, and the spring where their finder first washed them. One of Hyginus' fables tells it otherwise: Antiope had been Lycus' own wife, put away after the Sicyonian seduced her by a trick; Jupiter came to her afterwards, and Dirce, whom Lycus married next, suspected her husband of lying with Antiope in secret and kept her bound in darkness until Jove's will freed her. Labour took her at a crossroads — whence Zethus' name, from 'seeking' a place, and Amphion's, from a birth 'about the road'.

chapters.title: Dirce and the bull
chapters.text: Zethus grew up tending cattle and Amphion singing to a lyre Hermes gave him, while Lycus and his wife Dirce kept Antiope shut away in torment. One day her bonds fell loose of themselves and she fled to her sons' farmstead. In Apollodorus they knew her; in Hyginus, retelling Euripides, Zethus turned her away as a runaway slave, until Dirce, come there in Dionysus' revels, seized her for death and the herdsman told the youths she was their mother. They lashed Dirce to a bull, and her body was thrown into the spring that bears her name — or, by Liber's favour, became it. Apollodorus has Lycus killed, Pausanias beaten in battle; in Hyginus Mercury stays the brothers' hands and bids Lycus yield the kingdom to Amphion.

chapters.title: The walls of Thebes
chapters.text: So the twins won Thebes, which Lycus had held for twenty years, and Laius went into exile — to Pelops, in Apollodorus. Homer says the brothers were the first to found seven-gated Thebe and ring it with towers, since for all their strength they could not dwell there unwalled; Pausanias took them to have joined a lower town to Cadmus' citadel. On Jason's cloak Apollonius pictures Zethus shouldering a mountain peak while a boulder twice as large trails Amphion's golden lyre, and in Apollodorus too the stones follow the lyre. Zethus married Thebe, who gave the city her name; Amphion married Niobe, who in Ovid glories in the walls his strings had raised.

chapters.title: Two graves
chapters.text: Neither house lasted. Leto's children shot down Amphion's sons and daughters after Niobe's boast — though Pausanias' list of Theban kings blames a plague — and Zethus lost his son by the error of the boy's own mother: Homer's Penelope recalls the nightingale, Pandareus' daughter, mourning Itylus, son of lord Zethus, whom she killed unwitting. Zethus died of grief, and the Thebans brought Laius home to rule. The brothers share one mound at Thebes, set with rough stones said to be those Amphion's song once drew. Antiope, maddened by Dionysus for Dirce's fate, wandered Greece until Phocus son of Ornytion healed and married her; the people of Tithorea, where the two are buried, try to steal earth from the twins' mound when the sun is in Taurus, so that their own harvest, not Thebes', may thrive.
